summary: Analyzes the security exposure that arises when CAPWAP splits the traditional access point into separate parts that may communicate across hostile network hops, focused on IEEE 802.11 deployments. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: If the boss computer and the wifi box talk over a road that bad guys can reach, they might listen in or lie. This memo lists what could go wrong.

questions: security of centralized wireless access point control
what attacks can dtls prevent in capwap
subtitle: Security risks of splitting a wireless access point across a network.

tldr.problem: Splitting wireless access points into separate components (a controller and radio units) introduces security risks because sensitive protocol interactions that were once local are now transmitted over untrusted networks.
tldr.mechanism: The analysis identifies threats from passive and active attackers, covers deployment scenarios, and evaluates how DTLS (Datagram TLS) can secure the communication between components.
tldr.outcome: DTLS mitigates most risks, but cannot prevent denial-of-service attacks, passive monitoring, or traffic analysis. Operators must deploy controls appropriate to their threat environment.

today: RFC 5418 is Informational and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the threat analysis for CAPWAP in IEEE 802.11 environments. CAPWAP itself is specified in RFC 5415 and RFC 5416.

sections.title: How CAPWAP Splits the Access Point
sections.content:
Wireless access points (APs) traditionally combine two roles: handling wireless radio signals from clients and managing connections to the wired network. CAPWAP (Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points) splits these roles into two parts, a Wireless Termination Point (WTP) that handles the radio link, and an Access Controller (AC) that manages policy and client authentication. The AC and WTP communicate over an IP network that may not be physically secure. This document analyzes the security implications of that split for IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi) deployments.

The central challenge is that security-critical operations—such as authenticating clients and distributing cryptographic keys—happen inside the split now. If an attacker can reach the AC-WTP link, they can eavesdrop on these exchanges, impersonate either component, or modify control messages. The analysis considers both passive adversaries (who only listen) and active attackers (who can inject or modify traffic).
sections.eli5: A traditional wifi box does radio stuff and network stuff in one box. CAPWAP puts the radio stuff in one box and the network stuff in another box far away. If bad guys can access the network between them, they can spy or trick the boxes.

sections.title: Adversaries and Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC considers six deployment scenarios: localized networks within a single building; internet hotspots where the AC may be cloud-based; large organizations with centralized or distributed controllers; campus networks with outdoor WTPs; branch office deployments where the AC is at headquarters; and telecommuter scenarios where WTPs send traffic back to the office over the internet. Each scenario presents different risks depending on network trust and physical security.

Two classes of attackers are analyzed: passive adversaries who observe and record traffic but cannot inject packets, and active adversaries who can inject, modify, delete, or reflect packets. Active attackers are subdivided into pass-by attackers (who inject locally, using techniques like DNS poisoning) and man-in-the-middle (MitM) attackers who sit directly on the AC-WTP path and can do anything with the traffic they see.
sections.eli5: The memo describes six different ways wifi networks are set up—some in one building, some spread across cities, some sending traffic over the internet. It also lists what bad guys could do: some just listen, some pretend to be the AC or WTP, some change the messages.

sections.title: Threats from the Split
sections.content:
When the AP functions split, several new attack surfaces appear. During discovery (when a WTP finds an AC), an attacker can redirect the WTP to a fake AC, flood the AC with spurious discovery requests to cause denial of service, or modify discovery messages to mislead the WTP into believing the AC has different capabilities than it actually has. During association (when the WTP joins the AC), attackers can inject malformed setup messages, impersonate either end, or modify configuration data.

Once connected, the vulnerabilities shift. A passive attacker can eavesdrop on tunneled client data and learn who is using the network, what they are doing, and what security they employ. An active attacker with MitM capability can modify user data, change control messages to alter WTP configuration or load malicious firmware, or cause connection hijacking by assuming the identity of one endpoint. The RFC also notes that because CAPWAP involves multiple trust relationships (WTP-AC, AC-AAA server, client-AAA server), a compromise anywhere in the chain can affect the whole system.
sections.eli5: Bad guys could trick the wifi box into talking to a fake boss computer, or the boss computer into accepting a fake wifi box. They could change the secret keys for clients, redirect their data, or learn everything they are doing.

sections.title: Securing the AC-WTP Link
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five security properties that mitigate these threats: mutual authentication (each side proves it is who it claims), data-origin authentication (verifying messages came from the claimed sender), integrity verification (detecting if messages were altered), anti-replay protection (rejecting duplicate old messages), and confidentiality (encryption). All five are necessary for both control and data channels.

DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) provides all five properties. It supports mutual authentication using either pre-shared keys or X.509 certificates, binds message authentication to prior authentication, detects modifications, includes sequence numbering to reject replays, and offers strong encryption. When DTLS protects both the control channel (used for discovery, association, and provisioning) and the data channel (which carries tunneled client traffic and IEEE 802.11 management frames), it mitigates nearly all CAPWAP-specific vulnerabilities introduced by splitting the AP.
sections.eli5: The solution is a security protocol called DTLS that makes the messages between the wifi box and boss computer secret, proves who is sending each message, and makes sure nobody changes them in transit. It is like sending sealed, signed, numbered letters instead of postcards.

sections.title: What DTLS Cannot Prevent
sections.content:
Despite DTLS's strength, the RFC identifies five remaining risks. Denial-of-service attacks can still occur—an attacker can initiate thousands of DTLS handshakes simultaneously to exhaust memory on the AC, or flood encrypted garbage to waste CPU cycles decrypting it, or use a MitM position to drop or reorder packets in ways difficult to detect. Passive monitoring (sniffing) cannot be prevented by the protocol; only encryption mitigates it, and DTLS encryption does not prevent traffic analysis (deducing patterns from message sizes and timing). An active MitM can also mount attacks that are hard to detect, such as selectively deleting packets or delaying them. Finally, attacks like DNS poisoning or DHCP spoofing are beyond CAPWAP's scope entirely.

The RFC recommends operational controls to address the gaps: rate-limiting session initialization, auditing and alerting on events that exceed packet-loss thresholds, monitoring for performance degradation, and ensuring network infrastructure like DHCP and DNS are secured by operational means. For the highest-risk deployments (such as telecommuters sending traffic over the public internet), deploying an additional VPN between the WTP and AC is advisable.
sections.eli5: DTLS stops spies and liars, but not everything. Bad guys could still flood the boss computer with fake connection requests, watch how much data moves without reading it, or selectively break messages. The RFC says to add extra rules like rate limits and watches for these cases.
